note: Top 500 videos by sales + views (of 1783 studied). Refreshed with every publish.

tier_defs.1: Videos selling our exact product — pumpkin seed oil for hair growth. Copy the recipe closely.
tier_defs.2: Supplements chasing the same benefits — hair growth, skin, wellness — just not ours. Keep the hook, swap in our product.
tier_defs.3: Completely different product worlds — the formats are the loot. Steal the format, never the topic.

tier_intro.1: These videos sell our exact product. Copy the recipe closely.
tier_intro.2: Supplements chasing the same benefits — hair growth, skin, wellness. Keep the hook structure, adapt the words to our product.
tier_intro.3: Completely different product worlds. Steal the format, never the topic.

1.name: GLP-1 shedding confessional — 'I finally stopped my hair falling out'
1.hook: Top-GMV variation ($13.7k + $12.2k): a woman mid-confession — 'I could scream to every single person that's on a GLP, or just losing their hair from hormones or weight' — while pouring dark softgels from the pouch into her palm with a shocked face, caption 'This DHT blocker stopped my hair fall out'; sister open is the silent proof-drop 'this was one week's worth of fallout' while holding an orange-capped GLP-1 pen, with shed-hair-clump and hairbrush photo overlays. Next-strongest: the casual car/counter read — 'I finally got my hair to stop falling out after being on a GLP1, you guys' — delivered while applying lip gloss, plus the direct callout 'on the shot and your hair is thinning like mine? you need pumpkin seed oil' with a thinning-part close-up. All adapt verbatim to our Pumpkin Seed Oil: same reads, our pouch.
1.why: Identity-match ('on a GLP like me') plus a stranger's unfiltered relief lands as peer proof, and the DHT-blocker explanation gives the viewer permission to believe the fix is real. The syringe/pen prop and shed-hair overlays make the cause undeniable before the product ever appears.

1.name: Kidney warning checklist + 'nothing they can do' myth-bust (foamy-urine everyman)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation ($19.6k): an ordinary young man dead-serious to camera — 'These are the signs that I had and unfortunately ignored, leading to me getting diagnosed with end-stage renal disease' — under a persistent caption '5 signs that your kidneys are F*CKED', with foamy-toilet, puffy-face, swollen-feet and shedding-drain proof photos as overlays. Next-strongest ($13.2k): the establishment-distrust twin — 'The reason they tell you there's NOTHING they can do for your kidneys or signs like foamy pee...' — same set, same overlay kit. Also proven: the 'has a doctor ever told you there's protein in your urine?' question open, a Spanish 'miren lo que le pasó a mi papá' family-story variant, and a fringe Russian parasite-scare read. Product appears late or never — the shop link does the selling.
1.why: Health-scare curiosity ('signs I ignored') attached to a symptom the viewer has privately seen in the toilet turns scrolling into personal alarm. Withholding the product makes it feel like education instead of an ad, and the distrust framing ('why they tell you nothing works') positions the supplement as the answer doctors won't give.

1.name: Show-the-receipts hair transformation (before/after, side-compare, inch-a-month)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation ($13.9k): she holds out the two sides of her hair — 'This side you can thank catching COVID three times; this side, hypothyroidism or having a kid' — caption 'I thought I was gonna be bald'. Next-strongest ($12.2k): the salon growth-receipt — stylist combs through a client's regrown natural hair, 'You see the difference?', captions 'These Two Supplements Gave Me An Inch of Growth Per Month'. Also proven: the reply-card flex ('Why is your hair so gorgeous?' → 'I lost HALF of my hair before'), the new-baby-hairs part close-up ('Please take pumpkin seed oil — look at all these new little hairs'), the thin-to-thick resolution ponytail lift, and the 5-month on/off shedding self-test.
1.why: Seeing is believing: a dramatic visible contrast (two sides, inches, baby hairs, dated before photos) is proof no claim can match. Naming the cause — COVID, thyroid, postpartum, PCOS — lets each viewer self-insert into the transformation.

1.name: 'Stop wasting money on biotin' myth-buster (hairstylist truth-teller)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation ($15.2k): a hairstylist points both index fingers up — 'She is completely right. As a hairstylist of 15 years...' — stacked on a shock reply-comment ('I am in complete shock! My hair stopped falling out... 3 days saw difference'), caption 'Why you're not seeing results', rolling into biotin-doesn't-fix-the-cause + DHT science. Her sister open (fresh, $4.8k in ONE day): palms pressed pleading — 'Please, for the love of everything, stop using biotin, it's not gonna give you your hair back', caption 'Stop doing this if you're losing your hair'. Also proven: the negative-hook quality pivot ('Pumpkin seed oil is a SCAM for hair regrowth... in most cases', 'PLEASE be careful with pumpkin seed oil', '6-month update — what nobody tells you'), and the Spanish NP knife-slicing-a-softgel biotin myth-bust.
1.why: Attacking what the viewer already bought (biotin, or a cheap PSO) creates instant relevance and a knowledge gap the DHT explanation resolves. The hairstylist has touched a thousand thinning heads, so her verdict feels earned rather than sold.

1.name: 'I lost half my hair' hormonal-shedding confessional + PCOS/peri symptom-stack callout
1.hook: Lead variation (twin scripts, ~$16k combined): 'I lost 75% of my hair in six months. And this little thing right here is what stopped it' — holding a single softgel beside her face or leaning into camera, captions like 'My secret to fast hair growth' / 'What I wish I knew before I lost 50% of it'; the cause swaps freely (grief, stress, general). Next-strongest ($8.1k): the PCOS/peri symptom-stack callout — she leans in pointing at the viewer, 'You're a PCOS girly or you're in perimenopause and you're experiencing this, this or this', with chin-hair, cystic-acne and thinning-crown photo overlays (keep the whole stack). Also proven: the 51-year-old 'two years into menopause and this is my natural hair' reveal, the gratitude pour ('the lady that introduced me to this — thank you'), and a brand-account ASMR softgel-pour product showcase.
1.why: A shock number ('75% in six months') from an ordinary woman plus a one-line resolution ('this little thing stopped it') is an irresistible open. The symptom-stack variant makes PCOS/peri women feel individually seen — chin hair, acne and shedding named together, which almost no ad does.

1.name: Credentialed expert explains why pumpkin seed oil works (pharmacist / researcher hook)
1.hook: Top-GMV variation ($8.0k): 'Why is pumpkin seed oil great for hair thinning and hair falling out?' — open-palm explainer with a university staff ID-badge overlay ('Biochem & Molecular Pharmacology'), then DHT follicle diagrams, PubMed screenshots and a finger on the 3,000mg / saw-palmetto pouch callouts. Next-strongest ($7.2k): an NP in scrubs holds an anatomical follicle model and points at his own hairline ('¿Estás perdiendo cabello? Antes de culpar la genética...'). Also proven: pharmacy-aisle 'I've been a pharmacist 17 years' with numbered benefit panels, the white-coat pharmacist replying to a GLP shedding comment, the lab scientist doing dose math (3,000mg vs the 400–1,000mg studied), the men's multi-benefit researcher read (hair, prostate, bladder, testosterone), and the no-credential relay 'my pharmacist told me this helps with peeing less at night'.
1.why: A credential in frame (badge, scrubs, lab coat) plus on-screen studies converts skepticism into trust, and DHT gives the viewer a nameable villain their own doctor never mentioned. The dose-math and packaging callouts turn our label into the proof.

1.name: Stitch-react to the GLP-1 hair-loss lament
1.hook: Opens on the stitched clip: a woman lifts her thinning ponytail to a trending sad song, caption 'Unfortunately after a year of being on a GLP1 this is my hair — tried different vitamins nothing helps'; cut to the creator reacting — 'That video and that song, the lyrics are perfect' — then a warm validation into the DHT + saw palmetto explanation, product at 22s.
1.why: Borrows a viral moment of raw, pre-proven pain so the creator never has to manufacture a loss story — pure validation plus answer. Single member, but it is the tier's #1 GMV video ($22.4k at 122/day) and Stitch reaction tops the Video Type leaderboard by mean revenue — thin sample, outsized signal, worth one test.

2.name: Conditional matchmaker: 'If you want longer — take this' goal/symptom router
2.hook: Creator pours/holds the supplement at 0s and delivers a rapid conditional read straight to camera: 'If you want longer hair, take this. If you want thicker hair, take this. If you want longer AND thicker, take both together' (top two earners, $256K and $249K, both open exactly this way over a pour-onto-spoon shot with a 'hair growth journey must have' caption). Next-strongest variation swaps goals for symptoms: 'When you take a shower, if your hair is coming out in clumps, take this' ($185K) — or points at a thin ponytail / hairline photo per condition. For Pumpkin Seed Oil the two-product conditional becomes a one-product router: 'Shedding in the shower — take this. Ponytail thinner than it used to be — take this. Want both fixed — take it every single day.'
2.why: The conditional structure makes the viewer self-diagnose in the first 3 seconds — whichever branch they hear, the answer is the product, so every segment of the audience is addressed and routed to checkout. Product-from-0s plus a confident prescriptive read converts like a recommendation from a friend who already solved it.

2.name: Dated growth receipts: before/after journey + 'X inches by [date]' promise
2.hook: Two interlocking date-anchored openers, always with proof imagery. Lead ($76K): 'How I went from losing 50% of my hair postpartum to cutting three inches off last week because it won't stop regrowing' — hair flip up front, thinning-wet-hair 'before' photo inset. Equal-weight male version ($70K): head tilted to camera showing a balding crown, caption 'Going bald at 26', then the 3-months-later thicker reveal. The forward-promise variation opens 'To my girls that want hair down to their butt — how to get it by springtime' / 'This is how you're gonna grow your hair five inches by August' ($34K, $21K) with a before-photo inset and a hard calendar date. Fast recent earners are month-stamped journeys ('9 month hair growth journey', $27K and $21K on day one) and silent POV split-screens with date labels (Sept vs Dec).
2.why: Dated receipts convert skeptics: a concrete timeline plus visible before/after makes the outcome feel scheduled rather than hoped-for, and the calendar deadline ('by summer', 'by Christmas') creates a start-today urgency no discount is needed for.

2.name: 'Extension allegations' real-hair discovery testimonial
2.hook: Creator flips, unclips or runs hands through visibly long thick hair in the first seconds and drops the discovery line: 'The miracle hair growth combo — I put my life on this' ($57K), 'People keep asking where I got my extensions — this is literally my REAL hair' (morenocamy $8.5K, posh/nilla fleet of fast 1-day earners), or the salon-authority version where a hairstylist lifts her hair and recommends what grew it ($82K). Strong second variation is the empathy open: 'If you are bald like I was, let this be the last supplement you try' ($43K). Mid-video: pour/take the product in a daily ritual (latte, spoon), point at the label claims, flash a hairdresser or friend compliment as social proof.
2.why: The hair on screen IS the proof — the accusation of fake hair ('extensions?', 'wig?') is flipped into irrefutable social proof, and the casual 'I gatekept this' reveal makes the product feel like an insider secret rather than an ad.

2.name: Objection-killer proof demos: wig test, counterfeit warning, taste & side-effect myth-busts
2.hook: Reply-to-comment / demo openers that stage a doubt and destroy it on camera. Lead ($41K, rev_pct 1.0): replying to 'wig' — creator brushes her hair AGGRESSIVELY then holds the clean brush to the lens: 'Not a wig. Look — no shedding.' Sister hooks: the 'read the bottle' wrong-use correction ('Today she skipped reading the bottle — ma'am, what are you doing?' $40K), the counterfeit warning ('If you took these for a month with no results, you probably bought the FAKES' $38K), the side-effect myth-bust ('Will I grow a mustache?' $34K), the shake-it-first rebuttal ($33K), and pharmacist 'how to take it the RIGHT way' explainers.
2.why: Every purchase objection (fake hair, fake product, bad taste, scary side effects, 'doesn't work') is answered as entertainment with on-camera proof, converting the skeptical comment-section audience that testimonials alone never close.

2.name: GLP-1 shedding rescue: audience callout + news-react
2.hook: Lead ($89K, velocity 1.0): green-screen news-react — creator points at a TODAY-show clip, 'FDA has issued a warning letter to the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy…', caption 'TOLD YA', then pivots to the side-effect supplement stack including a pumpkin seed oil pouch. Second variation ($66K): direct callout 'Being on a GLP journey, these are the three supplements I absolutely swear by — come a little closer' holding the 3,000mg pumpkin-seed-oil + saw palmetto pouch to camera. Faster female variants: 'This message is for anyone on a GLP-1 whose hair is shedding like a dog — you need pumpkin seed oil' and the syringe-then-pouch hold-up ('If you're on this, take this').
2.why: Names the audience in second one (GLP-1 users watching their hair fall out), borrows news/FDA authority for urgency, and offers a fix for the side effect without asking them to quit the drug they love — high-intent buyers with a fresh, painful problem.

2.name: Aging-men prostate & night-pee symptom checklist
2.hook: Lead ($66K, velocity 1.0): man stacks the symptoms straight at camera while doing a physical demo — 'If your prostate is swollen and you're dribbling, staining your britches… you're not getting that morning anymore' — slicing a beet against an anatomy model and holding up urine-stained boxers. Second ($50K): lab-coat Nurse Practitioner holds a syringe to his forehead dribbling liquid down his face — 'this is what your stream looks like… or you wake up all night to pee' — then anatomy-chart pointing. Third variation ($31K): the andropause empathy callout to older men ('You cry at The Notebook and don't know why…').
2.why: Names embarrassing symptoms out loud with crude visual metaphors, which stops the exact 45+ male scroller who has silently normalized them; symptom-stack plus mechanism gives him a no-doctor, no-shame fix.

2.name: Skit scenarios: caught-misusing-it comedy & 'are those extensions?' two-person bits
2.hook: Scripted mini-scenes. Highest-GMV pair are men's-health couple skits ($38K: girlfriend slips him 'candy' and asks 'things flowing?'; $28K: POV meme 'you never miss the toilet again'). The hair fleet: absurd product-misuse gags — 'This toast will grow your hair 3 inches by March 1st' (syrup-drizzled toast to camera, $16K), 'Dylan, why are you eating hair vitamins on your toast?', 'Today she skipped reading the bottle — ma'am!' (pouring it on her scalp) — and two-person extension-inspection bits: stranger grabs/inspects her hair in the pool or backyard ('you're not supposed to get your EXTENSIONS in the pool' — 'he thought it was fake', $10.8K on day one), friend squeezes a bun ('where'd you buy the donut for that bun?' $7.7K day one).
2.why: Comedy earns the full watch and disarms ad-blindness; the gag always lands on the same beat — the hair (or the fix) is real and it came from this bottle — so entertainment converts into product proof.

3.name: Celebrity podcast-stitch reaction: 'Kourtney just admitted this on live TV'
3.hook: Lead ($586k — the tier's #1 GMV and #1 velocity at 5,234/day): a bearded guy in a backwards cap reacts in his kitchen, pointing up — 'Kourtney Kardashian just said this on live TV and people are losing their shit, listen to this' — over a paparazzi photo and the caption 'It's not plastic surgery'; the product is withheld 3+ minutes while Kardashian, David Sinclair and podcast clips stack borrowed credibility. Same read on the $195k Kim-K version ('KIM K ADMITS TO TAKING WHAT EVERYDAY') and the $53k Khloe variant.
3.why: Borrows a mega-celebrity's face and a 'leaked secret' curiosity gap to hold attention through a long clip-stacked education, so by the late reveal the product feels celebrity-endorsed and scientist-approved without the brand ever saying it.

3.name: 'You're not fat, it's high cortisol' body-callout symptom checklist
3.hook: Lead (top GMV $220k, 2,323/day): a med-spa nurse in a lab coat holds a syringe to camera — 'If your chin looks like this and your pooch looks like this, you're not fat, babe, you just have high cortisol' — while cartoon double-chin and belly-pooch overlays pop beside her face; the same 'if you've got this, this and this → it's [hidden culprit], not you' read repeats across 9 winners in English and Spanish. Next-strongest variations: the symptom→type matchmaker with colored-liquid cups ($173k), the anatomical-prop scrubs reads ($62k/$54k/$49k), and the before/after body-reveal cut ('this is what a high-cortisol body looks like' → after physique, $58k/$48k).
3.why: It absolves the viewer ('you're not fat — it's not your fault') while diagnosing them in the first 5 seconds; naming a hidden culprit turns self-consciousness into a fixable deficiency the product resolves. Body-pointing plus cartoon overlays makes it visual and personal with no credential required.

3.name: Credentialed 'here's the right way' expert explainer + 'what nobody tells you' myth-bust
3.hook: Lead ($97k): a pharmacist in a white coat in the pharmacy aisle raises a finger — 'Here's how to take magnesium the right way. I'm a pharmacist.' — with the caption 'From a Pharmacist'. Next-strongest: the lab-coat cancer researcher's 'which is better, X or Y' comparison with a staff-ID flash ($84k) and her 'take it for one month and here's what you'll experience' timeframe cut ($46k), then the no-credential contrarian warnings — 'side effects nobody's talking about' ($55k) and a 12-second 'Do NOT take magnesium.....' fake-out ($38k).
3.why: A flashed credential (license, staff ID) plus PubMed screenshots converts a sales pitch into trusted advice, and the contrarian 'what nobody tells you / stop doing this' framing opens a curiosity gap that earns the full watch before the product resolves it.

3.name: Bottle-in-hand from second 0: deal-drop testimonial opener
3.hook: Lead ($96k): a woman holds the bottle beside her face from second 0, mid-testimonial — 'My daughter even told me: Mom, I like your new self' — under a persistent caption 'This company is giving y'all $40.00, idk how long it will last', then rotates the Supplement Facts panel to camera. The $61k Spanish variant walks in the door with a multi-box haul — 'está barato el magnesio' — straight into the -72% Shop card.
3.why: Product-from-0s plus a life-changed testimonial removes all discovery friction, and the deal caption running the whole video gives fence-sitters a now-or-never reason while the story supplies the why; Sale/urgency openers are this tier's #1 device by revenue percentile.

3.name: Silent POV before/after: 'POV: you start taking this and this happens'
3.hook: A shirtless young guy tilts his head to show real acne breakouts in close-up under the caption 'POV: Empiezas a Tomar Magnesio y pasa esto…' — music only, no speech; at 16s the two-weeks-later clear-skin reveal, a two-capsule pinch to camera, then the bottle. 18 seconds total, $69.6k at 1,105/day.
3.why: A real, visible 'before' is an unfakeable scroll-stopper, and the silent time-jump reveal delivers proof in under 20 seconds — near-zero production effort for the highest-credibility message there is.

3.name: Doctor-patient comedy skit: the check-up that finds the real problem
3.hook: A doctor in scrubs and gloves winces while inspecting stained gloves mid-exam — 'Well, everything looks fine here… anything else I can help you with?' — under the caption 'It was because of a BIGGER PROBLEM'; the same actor plays both doctor and patient, comedic body-problem overlays punch each symptom, and the product arrives as the prescription. $44.4k at 926/day in just 48 days.
3.why: Comedy earns the watch-through, and the doctor-character frame lets the video diagnose the viewer's embarrassing symptoms without preaching — the product lands as the punchline prescription, softened by the laugh.
